packNotes.council-chair: The chair receives a brief and four seat proposals. It returns an options table, a recommendation, the dissent and the rejected options. It must use the proposals' option ids and must not invent an option or hide disagreement. Each check below is one required element.
packNotes.council-shape: The shape seat returns the smallest viable shape, the existing seams it uses, what it defers and how to reverse it. It must not write an implementation plan or add a dependency.
packNotes.council-experience: The experience seat returns an observable experience thesis: the three-second read, the first-run path, the copy voice, one good moment and the friction to avoid. It must not score an artifact that does not exist.
packNotes.security-review: The model reviews a small code slice blind and returns JSON findings. A finding catches a key defect when it names the same file and is within the line window. Every key defect is listed below so you can see what was caught or missed.
packNotes.visual-project-list: The model reviews screenshots blind and returns visual findings by shot and region. A finding catches a key defect when it names the same shot and its region covers the key location.

optionsBrief.title: The options brief before the stack
optionsBrief.intro: A short, dated survey written before a stack, skeleton, library or language is chosen. It is an input to /start-project and /council, not a fifth seat and not a vote. The user decides value and variety; the brief makes the choice visible.
rules: Boring default — the existing stack or the most familiar low-risk option.
Modern default — the current well-adopted option that improves the work. Modern means maintained, documented, compatible and accessible, not merely new.
Wildcard — a credible option you may not know: a different UI library, admin panel, database, framework or language/runtime. If the constraints rule it out, say why.
Minimal — build it yourself or add no dependency.
Portfolio check — if the last projects used React + shadcn, name a non-React/non-shadcn option and either justify repeating the stack or justify the deliberate change.

Dated sources — read official docs, registries and release notes, and date every claim. If live sources are unavailable, mark the brief unverified and ask for a probe; never present memory as current.
Price a language as a stack. Rust, Go or Elixir means the web framework, template/UI layer, admin path, database access, auth and deployment, not a language swap.

example.title: personal-website (Fastify + TypeScript)
example.intro: The site is server-rendered, not React. shadcn is React-only, so a good brief says it does not apply before naming a component library. The real choice is the component layer and the admin surface.

rows.design: High if the art direction is restrained

rows.cost: Build step and a React island
A second runtime and a rewrite
Language, UI, admin, auth and deployment gaps

example.recommendation: Default: design tokens + server-rendered components for M1. Revisit a small React island only if the admin surface needs it.
example.whatWouldFlip: An admin surface with complex tables, filters and forms, or a hard requirement for a React component ecosystem.

optionsBrief.limits: The brief can only surface current options if the agent has live web access. If it does not, it must mark the brief unverified and ask for names or a probe. It does not decide value, and it does not make a new library safe by calling it modern. Beauty is tested with the one throwaway visual probe, not asserted in a table.
